title: A window start computed as the window's index times its length proved equal to the remainder form
summary: Crosscut's `Window` counter computes the start of the window a reading falls in as `nowNanos - nowNanos % windowNanos`. A rewrite names the window's index first, `nowNanos / windowNanos`, and multiplies it back: the form a reader expects, and the one that gives the index a name for a log line or a key. The two are equal by Java's division identity, `d == (d / p) * p + d % p` for every `d` and `p`, which no engine proved within a minute until the tool's own checker learned it: a quotient times its divisor is now the dividend less the remainder, the same bits the old version computes, and the proof over every counter, reading and window takes 0.1 s.

change.description: Compute the window's index, `long index = nowNanos / windowNanos`, and its start as `index * windowNanos`, in place of `nowNanos - nowNanos % windowNanos`. The tests are unchanged.

risk: None: the proof is over every counter, clock reading and window length, the same result record or the same exception in both versions. What is at stake is the review of an arithmetic identity on 64-bit values, where a reader has to recall that Java's `/` truncates toward zero and `%` takes the dividend's sign, so that the identity holds for negative readings too (a clock reading from `System.nanoTime` can be negative).
explanation: The harness builds the counter from symbolic components, calls both versions on the same reading and window, and compares the result records component by component, or the exceptions by class. In the tool's own checker, `nowNanos / windowNanos` and `nowNanos % windowNanos` are one division left to the solver, with fresh bits for the quotient and remainder under what holds of every division; the product of that quotient and the divisor is not a multiplication at all but `nowNanos - remainder`, since `d == (d / p) * p + d % p` holds for every pair of values, so the new version's start is the old version's start, the same bits. The checker proves the harness in 0.1 s over 7 paths and 9 solver calls. JBMC, which has to relate a 64-bit divider to a 64-bit multiplier in one formula, did not finish within 60 s.
resolution: Merge. The named index reads better and the proof says it is the same window.
notes: No scope: the proof covers every input, the negative readings included, where both versions truncate toward zero (`-1 / 2 * 2` is 0, and `-1 - -1 % 2` is 0 too), and the inputs both versions refuse (a non-positive window, a reading before the start, a count that overflows into the constructor's check), where both throw `IllegalArgumentException`.

The tool's own checker rewrites a quotient times its divisor as the dividend less the remainder, `(a / b) * b` as `a - a % b`, exactly: the identity holds in two's complement for every pair, the division by zero (which the JVM throws on before the value matters) and `MIN_VALUE / -1` included. Both versions then compute the same bits for the start, and the comparison of the results folds to true before the solver is asked. The log (`bmc.log` in the work directory) says `0 of 0 multiplications built in full`: no product was left to the solver. Before the rewrite the checker did not finish this harness in two minutes, and example 133's last note records the same identity out of reach on the token bucket's credited time.

A product the identity does not cover is left to the solver, like a division: fresh bits under what holds of every product modulo the width (a factor of zero gives zero, of one the other factor, of minus one its negation, a power of two shifts, and the low eight bits are exact), with the multiplier built only where a model got a product wrong. Example 131's loop of `delay *= multiplier` on a multiplier of two went from 22 s to 4 s this way, none of its 27 products built, and example 139 is a product the facts settle by a factor of one.

JBMC, with its default solver, did not finish the same harness within 60 s: the identity over a 64-bit division and multiplication is where a SAT solver's unsatisfiability proof is slow, in JBMC and in this checker's circuits alike, which is why the checker does not build them for it. The reading `nowNanos / windowNanos * windowNanos` in one expression gives the same bits, the quotient being the same lazy division.

Gap scan (step 1a of `llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md`, 5 November 2026, JDK 25.0.4.1, from the bytecode, nothing proved): the tool's own checker meets no gap in the 2 methods the proof reaches in either version, so strict mode does not move this verdict.
provenance: Constructed as the divide-and-multiply form of the window alignment that example 137's last note left out of reach of both engines, on the same kernel of Crosscut, to show the tool's own checker proving the division identity by rewriting a quotient times its divisor.

references.title: The Java Language Specification, 15.17.2 and 15.17.3: division truncates toward zero and the remainder satisfies (a / b) * b + (a % b) == a
Cloudflare: How we built rate limiting capable of scaling to millions of domains (fixed windows aligned to the clock)
Godlin and Strichman, Regression verification: proving the equivalence of similar programs (2013)
